caseno: Civil Revision No. 5630 of 1991 (Dhaka) and Civil Revision No. 12 of 1988 (Jessore).
lawyer:
Shahabuddin Ahmad for Nizamuddin Haider, Advocates ----- For the Petitioner. 
Abdur Rahman with Syed Golam Mostafa, Advocates ----- For the Opposite Parties.
parties:
Shaikh Shamsuddin Ahmed ----- Petitioner.
Vs.
Nazmul Huda and others ----- Opposite Parties.
full_judgment:
This rule issued on an application under section 115 of the Code of Civil Procedure at the instance of the defendants is directed against the order passed on 6.1.88 by the Subordinate Judge, 2nd Court, Khulna adding two persons as opposite parties in Misc. Case No. 28 of 1982 under Order 9 rule 9 of the Code arising out of Title Suit No. 57 of 1974. 

 3. On 4.5.82 an application under Order 9 rule 9 of the Code bearing signatures of the name of the plaintiff was filed for setting aside the order of dismissal and it was registered as Misc. case No. 28 of 1982. Before filing written objection the contesting defendant on 14.3.83 filed a petition for directing personal appearance of the plaintiff petitioner pleading that the rehearing application was not filed by the plaintiff when had died long ago. The learned Judge having heard both sides allowed the prayer on 31.7.83 directing the plaintiff petitioner to appear personally in court an 12.9.83. On 8.8.83, however, Nazmul Huda, who is opposite Party No. 1 in this Revision case claiming himself to be the constituted attorney of the plaintiff appeared and filed a petition praying for amendment of the rehearing application accordingly. Subsequently, opposite party No. 3 Mosharraf Hasan and opposite party No. 4 Mokbul Hossain Khan of this Revision Case appeared on 8.2.84 and 29.2.84 respectively and filed petitions praying for their addition as petitioners in the rehearing case claiming interest in the suit property on the strength of Kabala purchase from the plaintiff through his attorney Nazmul Huda. These two petitions were rejected by the learned Subordinate Judge on, 11.3.84. Against this order Mosharraf and Mokbul Hussain Khan filed Misc. Appeal No. 53 of 1984 which was in due course dismissed by the learned District Judge on 17.4.85 with some observations and direction upon the trial Court as follows: 

 "The first and foremost point that the trial Court should decide since its order dated 14.3.83 is whether Jagannath Banerjee was alive at the time of filing of the Misc. Case under Order 9 rule, 9 CPC and whether he signed that Misc. petition or not. The question of substitution under rule 10 of Order 22 CPC may be considered only after the above point is finally decided in the affirmative on the personal appearance of Jagannath Banerjee before the trial Court and ascertained that he had signed the Misc. Petition. The learned Subordinate Judge be directed to consider afresh any petition filed by the petitioner under Order 22 rule 10 CPC after the question whether Jagannath Banerjee had filed the Misc. Petition under Order 9 rule 9 CPC has finally been decided in the affirmative". 

 4. On 30.5.85 Mosharraf Hasan and Mokbul Hussain Khan (appellants in the Misc. Appeal before the District Judge) filed two petitions before the trial Court for being added under Order 22 rule 10 in the Misc. Case. Subsequently, defendant Shamsuddin Ahmed filed a petition under Order 9 rule 12 CPC on 23.11.85 for rejection of the Misc. application on the ground that in spite of definite direction the plaintiff petitioner did not personally appear before the court. A copy of this petition was served on the other side on 21.11.85 and Nazmul Huda filed a written objection to the petition on 23.11.85 disclosing that "the petitioner filed this Misc. Case through his attorney. But due to mistake by oversight of the lawyer at the time of draft of the petition it was not written that Jagannath Banerjee represented through his attorney Nazmul Huda. "On 31.12.87, however Nazmul Huda submitted a death certificate showing that Jagannath Banerjee died on 16.11.83 in India. Ultimately the matter came up for decision before the trial Court which on hearing all concerned passed the impugned order on 6.1.88 allowing the petitions dated 30.5.85 filed by Mosharraf Hasan and Mokbul Hussain Khan under Order 22 rule 10 of the Code, holding that they acquired interest of Jagannath by purchase from him who as per the death certificate died on 16.11.83. 

 5. It has been urged by Mr. Shahabuddin Ahmad, the learned Advocate for the petitioner, that the learned Subordinate Judge has committed a serious error of law resulting in error in his decision occasioning failure of justice, in passing the impugned order without complying with the direction of the appellate Court, that is, the learned District Judge given in Misc. Appeal No. 53 of 1984. He submits that the addition of opposite parties Nos. 3 and 4 has been absolutely unwarranted before arriving at a firm decision as to whether the Misc. case was filed by the plaintiff Jagannath Banerjee. He has, however, raised a plea of abatement of the proceeding, but this does not seem to be so much relevant for the purpose of disposal of the instant matter. 

 7. The material observation and direction contained in the appellate judgment meant for guidance of the trial Court have already been quoted. Therein the trial Court is required in unambiguous terms to arrive at a firm decision as to whether Jagannath was alive at the time of filing of the Misc. Case and whether he signed the Misc. Application. It is that then and then only that the trial Court would be required to consider the application of opposite parties 3 and 4 to be filed afresh if they so desired (which they actually filed on 30.5.85). But the learned Subordinate Judge does not appear to have properly appreciated the observation and direction of the appellate Court. His decision has been based on wrong assumption which has been framed in the sentence:" 

 8. It will appear that the trial Court has not decided if Jagannath filed the Misc. application, and as such the consideration of the petition dated 30.5.85 of the opposite parties Nos. 3 and 4 has been in clear violation of the appellate Court's direction. It may be recalled that the learned Subordinate Judge proceeded rightly in compliance with the appellate Court's direction, vide his order dated 1.7.86. This approach was subsequently abandoned. Whatever that may be, it is clear that the trial Court has misdirected itself and committed an error of law in allowing the petitioners application dated 30.5.85. The error has definitely resulted in error in the decision to add opposite parties No. 3 and 4 in the Misc. Case. 

 9. Now the question is whether the erroneous decision has occasioned failure of justice. Mr. MA Rahim has referred to the decision in the case of Secretary, Ministry of Food. Vs. M/s. MF Limited reported in 44 DLR (AD) 166 to contend that the direction of the appellate Court was not mandatory and a mere technical irregularity has been committed by the court below in not complying with the direction. According to him, the addition of the parties will facilitate effective and complete determination of the controversy between the parties and as such no question of failure of justice arises at all. It must be pointed out that it cannot be conceived that the lower court has any option not to comply with the direction of the appellate Court which must always be taken to be mandatory. In the facts and circumstances the defendants by virtue of the appellate decision obtained a right to get decided the first question whether the rehearing case for setting aside the dismissal order which enured to their benefit can at all be maintained and without a decision thereon affirmatively the other side could not have their prayers for addition considered at all. In any view of the matter the direction of the appellate Court was mandatory for the trial Court and it was not merely a technical matter but a matter of substance going to the root of the question. The expression failure of justice is not capable of a very precise definition. It necessarily implies injustice suffered by a party as a consequence of a decision rendered by the court. In the instant case the defendant petitioner obtained the decision in his favour and against plaintiff Jagannath Banerjee. This decree of dismissal could not be set aside in the rehearing case by anybody other than the plaintiff. If the court embarks upon deciding the matter at the instance of a person who was not a party in the suit then certainly that would go to the root touching the merits of the case and in such view the defendant cannot be prejudiced by the decision. I must, therefore, hold that the erroneous decision arrived at by the court below has occasioned failure of justice. The decision cited by Mr. Rahim has no application to the instant case. The impugned order cannot, therefore, be maintained and is liable to be set aside. 

 The impugned order passed by the learned Subordinate Judge on 6.1.88 in Misc. Case No. 28 of 1988 is set aside. The learned Judge is directed to decide the matter afresh along with Nazmul Huda's petition dated 8.8.83 and Shamsuddin's petition and Nazmul Huda's written objection both dated 28.11.85 in accordance with law, in the light of the observations made above and in compliance with the direction of the appellate Court.
